title: The False Choice
objective: After this level you can spot a false dilemma that hides the options beyond the two on offer.
summary: A false dilemma offers too few options and demands a pick. Its flaw is a false premise: that these are the only choices. Escape by naming a missing option; a genuinely complete menu is fine.

cards.headline: A toaster with two settings: burnt and off.
cards.body: It's a joke because you know toasters do better than that. Arguments pull the same move with a straight face, and there it's no joke. Shrink the menu to two options, one of them awful, and you can steer someone to the one you wanted.

cards.headline: Too few options
cards.body: A false dilemma unfairly offers too few choices, then insists you pick one. With just two, it's also called a false dichotomy or the black-or-white fallacy. "Either you love this band or you have no taste" ignores liking a few of their songs, or just preferring jazz. The flaw sits in a premise: the claim that these are the only options.

cards.headline: Going between the horns
cards.body: One example in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy is a pollster asking whether your boss is drunk on the job once a week, twice a week or more. What about never? Picture the options as the horns of a charging bull. Name a choice the menu left out, and you slip between the horns, ungored.

cards.headline: Not every either/or is false
cards.body: Some choices really are two-way. "Will you give $20 or won't you?" is fair: those are the only options. So the test is whether the menu is complete, not whether it's short. A neat way to remember it: everything is either black or not black, but not everything is either black or white.

cards.headline: False choice: spotted
learned: A false dilemma offers too few options
Its flaw: "these are the only choices"
Escape by naming a missing option

questions.prompt: What does a false dilemma do?

options.label: Attacks the person making the argument
Offers too few options and demands a pick
Offers so many options you cannot choose
options.rationale: The trouble is too few options, not too many.

options.label: Twists the other side into a weaker version

questions.explanation: A false dilemma unfairly limits the choices, often to two, then insists you choose among them.

questions.prompt: Match each either/or question with its verdict.

pairs.left: Will you give $20 or won't you?
You love this band or you have no taste
Once a week, twice a week or more

questions.explanation: "Will you give $20 or won't you?" is fair: those really are the only options. The band choice and the pollster's "once a week, twice a week or more" are false dilemmas that leave options out.

questions.prompt: "Either you love this band or you have no taste" relies on the unstated premise that _____.

options.label: jazz is better than this band
options.rationale: That's one of the options it ignores.

options.label: these are the only two options

questions.explanation: A false dilemma quietly needs the premise that nothing lies between its two options. Say it out loud and it falls apart.
